turns.q:
Your response was: "Um, well, I—I noticed the way the totals are... I mean, the layout for the items is clear, but I'm not sure if the distinction between the prices is—sorry, that might be overthinking it. And then there’s the button area at the bottom; the "Continue Shopping" part feels very prominent, almost maybe too much? But again, I don't know if that's actually a design choice or just my own... well, I can't really say for sure. It's a lot to take in, so I—I might be misinterpreting the flow entirely."

We want to understand what you meant by "the "Continue Shopping" part feels very prominent, almost maybe too much?", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The large size and bold styling of the "Continue Shopping" button compared to the "Place Order" button.
B) The placement of the "Continue Shopping" option directly above the final checkout action.
C) The visual weight of the "Continue Shopping" section within the overall bottom navigation area.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: I... I think it's mostly A, I mean, it's probably option A. The way "Continue Shopping" is in that dark box makes it look so much more active than the "Place Order" button, which looks almost grayed out or like it might not even be clickable yet. It just feels like my eyes go straight to that first one... I'm sorry, I don't know if that's the right way to put it, but the contrast is very high for a secondary action.

turns.q: What specifically about the visual styling of the "Continue Shopping" box makes it stand out more than the "Place Order" button in this layout?
turns.a: I—well, I think it's mainly the contrast level... I mean, because the "Continue Shopping" button is in that very dark, solid black block, it has so much more visual weight. In comparison, the "Place Order" button is just this light gray, which makes it look almost like it’s disabled or not the primary action. It's possible they were trying to... well, maybe they wanted to make sure people didn't feel trapped in the checkout, but it does make the secondary option much more prominent than the final one.

turns.q: If a user encountered this layout for the first time, would that visual weight on "Continue Shopping" make the primary task of placing an order harder to identify?
turns.a: I—well, I think it might... well, it could definitely cause some hesitation. Because the "Place Order" button is so much lighter and almost blends into the background compared to that heavy black box above it, a user's eye is naturally pulled toward "Continue Shopping" first. It creates this sort of... well, it makes it feel like the secondary action is actually the primary one, which might make someone stop and wonder if they missed something or if the order button isn't actually active yet. I mean, I could be wrong, but it just feels less like a "final" step because of that contrast difference.

turns.q: When the "Place Order" button looks disabled or not like the primary action due to its light styling, what does that tell you about what the layout got structurally wrong?
turns.a: I—well, I think it suggests a bit of a mismatch in the hierarchy... I mean, because "Place Order" is clearly the main goal for this page, but the visual weight is actually on "Continue Shopping." It feels like the design might be accidentally signaling that the order isn't ready to be finalized yet. I'm not sure if it's a technical error or just a choice, but... well, it makes the primary path feel less certain than it should be for a checkout screen.

turns.q: What would need to be reorganized in this layout so that the "Place Order" button clearly stands out as the primary action?
turns.a: I—well, I think it might... well, if we just swapped the visual weight, that's one thing, but specifically, I think the "Continue Shopping" button shouldn't be such a large, solid block. It could maybe be styled more like a text link or a less heavy button so it doesn't compete with the "Place Order" action. And then... well, if the "Place Order" button had a darker background or a bolder border, it would probably feel much more like the final step. I'm not sure if that's too simple to say, but right now, the contrast just makes them seem almost equally important, which is confusing for a checkout flow.

turns.q: Since you mentioned the "Continue Shopping" button shouldn't be such a large, solid block to avoid competing with the primary action, how would changing that specific element affect a user's ability to identify the correct next step in this layout?
turns.a: I—well, I think it might... well, if "Continue Shopping" was less of a heavy block, it would probably clear up some of the confusion about what the primary goal is. Right now, because both are large buttons but only one is dark, it feels like there's a conflict in what the user should do next. If the secondary option were more subtle—maybe just a smaller button or even a text link—then the "Place Order" button would naturally stand out as the main path. I mean, I could be wrong about how people scan these things, but it would probably make the flow feel much more... well, intuitive, because the visual hierarchy wouldn't be pulling them away from finishing the purchase.

turns.q: If the design team could only change one structural thing before this went to development—what would actually make the difference for you in ensuring the "Place Order" button is clearly seen as the primary action?
turns.a: I—well, I think it might... well, if they just inverted the visual weight of those two bottom buttons. Specifically, making the "Place Order" button the one with the dark, solid background and then... well, maybe making "Continue Shopping" a much lighter, less prominent style like a ghost button or even just a text link. I mean, it's probably the most direct way to fix it because right now, the contrast is actually working against the user's goal of finishing the purchase. I—I'm sorry, that might be too simple a fix, but honestly, if they swapped those styles, the hierarchy would finally feel... well, it would just make sense for a checkout page.
